rungs.stem: In the Old English poem Beowulf, the young Geat hero has sailed to Denmark to help King Hrothgar defend his mead-hall Heorot from a monster that has been terrorising it every night for twelve years. What is the name of the monster Beowulf has come to fight?
choices: Grendel
Fafnir
Humbaba
Cerberus
rungs.context: Beowulf lines 86-193: the monster is Grendel, a descendant of Cain, who hates the sound of harp-song in Heorot and comes each night to devour Hrothgar's men. Fafnir is the Norse dragon on Gnitaheid. Humbaba is the forest-guardian killed by Gilgamesh. Cerberus is the three-headed hound guarding the Greek underworld. Grendel is the specific enemy of the poem's first half.

rungs.stem: Beowulf and his fourteen Geat thanes settle down in Heorot for their first night. Before lying down among his men to pretend to sleep, Beowulf makes a striking decision -- he refuses to prepare in the way any warrior of his time would prepare for a night attack. HOW does Beowulf plan to meet Grendel when the monster comes?
choices: bare-handed, with no weapon at all
with a sword blessed by Hrothgar
with a spear thrown from the doorway
with a torch to blind the monster
rungs.answer: bare-handed, with no weapon at all
rungs.context: Beowulf 677-687: Beowulf gives his sword away, takes off his mail-shirt and helmet, and lies down bare-handed. Warriors of his day would never sleep unarmed under monster-threat. The poet tells the reader the reason at once: Grendel scorns weapons and Beowulf will not shame his opponent with an advantage the monster cannot use.

rungs.stem: Beowulf has a very specific reason for setting his sword aside before Grendel comes. He tells his men that he will fight the monster in exactly the same way the monster fights. What is Beowulf's reason for going against Grendel unarmed?
choices: Grendel uses no weapons himself, and Beowulf takes no advantage
iron cannot cut Grendel's skin, so a sword is useless
his king has forbidden him to draw a blade in a foreign hall
his sword was lost overboard on the voyage to Denmark
rungs.answer: Grendel uses no weapons himself, and Beowulf takes no advantage
rungs.context: Beowulf 677-687: Beowulf refuses the advantage because Grendel scorns weapons. Iron does turn out to fail against Grendel's hide -- the poet mentions this LATER, after the fight -- but Beowulf's stated reason for lying down unarmed is honour, not futility. The other reasons are not in the poem.

rungs.stem: At midnight Grendel came stalking to Heorot from the moors. When he reached the mead-hall the first thing he did was tear one specific thing off with a single blow of his hand -- the poem lingers on this moment as the first proof of the monster's strength inside the walls. What did Grendel rip off in his first act inside Heorot?
choices: the great iron-bound door
the smoke-vent above the fire
the king's high seat
the harp from its peg
rungs.context: Beowulf 720-724: Grendel wrenches Heorot's iron-bound door off its hinges with one hand and strides in. The poet stresses the door's iron bands to make the ease of Grendel's entry more terrifying. The smoke-vent, king's seat, and harp are all real features of an Anglo-Saxon mead-hall but not what Grendel tears loose.

rungs.stem: Grendel came through the doorway and the first Geat he saw sleeping was closest to him. He did not fight the man; he ATE him on the spot before anyone else in the hall could rise. Later in the poem, when Beowulf retells the story to his own king Hygelac back in Geatland, the poet actually gives the eaten thane a name. What is the name of the Geat that Grendel ate first?
choices: Hondscioh
Wiglaf
Aeschere
Unferth
rungs.context: Beowulf 740-745 and 2076: the sleeping Geat Grendel devoured first is named Hondscioh, in the retelling to Hygelac. Wiglaf is the young thane who alone stays with Beowulf against the dragon fifty years later. Aeschere is Hrothgar's closest counsellor, killed by Grendel's mother the following night. Unferth is the Dane who taunts Beowulf at the feast.

rungs.stem: Grendel finished Hondscioh and reached for the next sleeping man. But that man was not asleep. Beowulf's own hand closed on Grendel in the grip that the poem returns to again and again -- Grendel found, the poet says, that in all the world he had NEVER met a match for what one specific part of Beowulf could do. What part of Beowulf's body did Grendel discover he could not match?
choices: Beowulf's hand-grip
Beowulf's shoulders
Beowulf's footwork
Beowulf's headbutt
rungs.context: Beowulf 749-753: 'that son of Cain found at once that in all the world he had never met a hand-grip mightier than his own.' The Old English word the poet uses is 'mundgripe', literally 'hand-grip', and it recurs seven times in the fight-scene. There is no spear and no sword in this fight; the whole substance of Beowulf's victory is the grip of his one hand on Grendel's one hand.

rungs.stem: The two of them WRESTLED UPRIGHT in the pitch-dark hall, so fiercely that a specific thing broke apart all around them -- the poet uses the destruction to show how the fight is shaking Heorot itself. What broke apart around Beowulf and Grendel as they wrestled in the darkness?
choices: the mead-benches burst from their pegs
the roof-beams sagged with the noise
the fire-pit collapsed in on itself
the wall-hangings caught fire from the torches
rungs.answer: the mead-benches burst from their pegs
rungs.context: Beowulf 767-771: the great mead-benches sprang from their iron pegs as the two fighters slammed against them. Everything else in the hall stayed standing, and Heorot did not burn until decades later. The bursting benches are the poet's single sound-and-vision cue for the fight's violence.

rungs.stem: Grendel realised he was trapped in a grip he could not break. Terrified for the first time in his monstrous life, he turned to flee back to his fen. But Beowulf would not let go, and Grendel PULLED AWAY with all his desperate strength -- and paid for the pull. What tore away from Grendel's body in Beowulf's grip as the monster wrenched to escape?
choices: his arm and shoulder, torn out at the socket
his three long claws, ripped from the fingertips
his lower jaw, snapped clean off the skull
his leg and hip, wrenched from the joint
rungs.answer: his arm and shoulder, torn out at the socket
rungs.context: Beowulf 815-818: Grendel's arm and shoulder tear off at the socket -- the poet describes tendons popping and the bone-locker bursting. Not the jaw, not the claws alone, not the leg. The specific violence of the whole shoulder coming off is the fight's climax and the image every reader of Beowulf remembers.

rungs.stem: Grendel fled from Heorot with his life-blood spurting into the night. He ran back the way he had come, across the moors, headed for one specific place he had always considered safe. Where did the wounded Grendel flee to die?
choices: his cave beneath the mere
the deep forest north of Heorot
the sea-cliffs of the Geat coast
the burial-barrow of his kin
rungs.context: Beowulf 819-836: Grendel dies in the cave he shares with his mother beneath a haunted mere (lake). Beowulf will follow him there the day after next to face Grendel's mother in the very cave. The Geat coast is Beowulf's homeland, not Grendel's. The burial-barrow of the dragon is a different location fifty years later.

rungs.stem: When morning came the Danes and Geats crowded into Heorot to see the proof of Beowulf's victory. Beowulf had hung the trophy in one specific place in the hall so that everyone entering could see it at once, and so that all the tribes of Denmark would come to view it. Where did Beowulf hang Grendel's torn-off arm as the trophy of his fight?
choices: from the rafters of Heorot
at the great door where Grendel had entered
on the king's high seat
outside the hall on a spear
rungs.context: Beowulf 833-836: 'under the vaulted roof' -- Beowulf hoisted Grendel's whole shoulder, arm, and clawed hand up into the rafters of Heorot to hang there as proof of the kill. The image is the most-remembered visual in all of Old English poetry: a monster's arm dangling from the mead-hall roof at dawn.

rungs.stem: The Beowulf poem, and the whole scene of Grendel's arm coming off in Heorot, has come down to us across a thousand years through a single object. In 1731 that object was nearly destroyed. What happened in 1731 that almost cost the world the Beowulf poem forever?
choices: a fire at Ashburnham House scorched the manuscript
a Danish raid burned the monastery library
a monk erased the vellum to reuse the parchment
a shipwreck lost the copy sent to France
rungs.answer: a fire at Ashburnham House scorched the manuscript
rungs.context: The Nowell Codex (Cotton Vitellius A.xv), containing the only copy of Beowulf, was in the Ashburnham House library when it caught fire on 23 October 1731. The manuscript survived but was scorched at the edges; every page has some fire-damage, and some words are lost to the burn. The Grendel-fight passage sits on folios 143r-146v of this single scorched book, now kept in the British Library.
